procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated April 16, 1969 of Madras High Court in Criminal Misc. Petitions Nos. 469 and 62I of 1969.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court rejected applications under s. 56 l A of the Cude of Criminal PrnccJure for quashing the proceedings against the appellants.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Two appeals by certificate (Criminal Appeals Nos. 18 and 19 of 1969) were initially allowed by the Supreme Court on July 23, 1969, setting aside the High Court's order. The current appeals (Criminal Appeals Nos. 113 and I63 of I969) are appeals from the Madras High Court judgment and order dated April 16, 1969. The Supreme Court dismissed these appeals.

issue.issue_text: Whether the complaint was not a bona fide one and had been filed with a collateral purpose to justify the unlawful detention of appellant no. 1.

facts: The appellant argued that the complaint filed against them was not a bona fide one.
It was contended that the complaint was filed with the collateral purpose of justifying the unlawful detention of appellant no. 1 (Schussler) in the country.
law: Under the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, the Director of Enforcement must first initiate adjudication proceedings (s. 23D) before filing a criminal complaint for contraventions of the Act.
A complaint for substantive offenses under the Act cannot be launched until the Director has made an inquiry and formed the opinion that a more drastic court conviction is necessary.
application: The Court found that the Director of Enforcement had not followed the mandatory procedure laid down in s. 23D of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act before filing the complaint.

The Court reasoned that it would be absurd to allow the Director to bypass this required procedure by simply filing a complaint for conspiracy under the Indian Penal Code (s. 120-B) when the alleged overt acts were contraventions of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act.
The Court's decision to quash the complaint was based entirely on this procedural failure.
While one judge expressed a personal opinion that the complaint was indeed not bona fide and was filed to justify the unlawful detention, this was not the legal basis for the Court's final decision.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument that the complaint should be quashed due to its lack of bona fides. Instead, the Court quashed the complaint on the separate procedural ground that the Director of Enforcement had failed to follow the mandatory adjudication process required by the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act before initiating the criminal proceedings.

issue.issue_text: Whether a complaint under s. 23 (I )(b) cannot be launched before the Director of Enforcement has taken up the adjudication proceedings and made some inquiry in those proceedings and formed the opinion that it was necessary to have resort to the more drastic provision of conviction by a court.

facts: A criminal complaint was filed by the Director of Enforcement against the appellants for alleged contraventions of the Act.
Prior to filing this complaint, the Director had not initiated or conducted any adjudication proceedings or inquiry against the appellants as prescribed by Section 23D of the Act.
law: The Supreme Court relied on its previous judgment in *M/s. Rayala Corporation (P) Ltd. & another v. The Director of Enforcement*.
Section 23D of the Act outlines the procedure for adjudication, requiring the Director of Enforcement to hold an inquiry.

A proviso in Section 23D(1) specifies that if, during the inquiry, the Director forms the opinion that the administrative penalty he is empowered to impose would be inadequate, he shall then make a complaint to a court.
application: The Court applied the precedent set in the *Rayala Corporation* case, which established a mandatory two-step process.
First, the Director of Enforcement must initiate adjudication proceedings and conduct an inquiry under Section 23D.

Second, only during the course of that inquiry can the Director form a considered opinion that the administrative penalty would be insufficient and that a more severe criminal prosecution under Section 23(1)(b) is necessary.

In the present case, this mandatory procedure was not followed. No adjudication proceedings had been started, and consequently, the Director could not have formed the requisite opinion based on an inquiry.

The Court reasoned that allowing the criminal complaint to proceed without following this statutory procedure would effectively nullify or "stultify" the provisions of Section 23(1)(b) and Section 23D.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court affirmed the principle that a criminal complaint under Section 23(1)(b) cannot be launched until the Director of Enforcement has first initiated adjudication proceedings under Section 23D, conducted an inquiry, and, based on that inquiry, formed the opinion that the available administrative penalty is inadequate and a court conviction is necessary. Since this procedure was not followed, the complaint was not maintainable at that stage.

issue.issue_text: Whether A 1 can be charged in respect of acts alleged against him in the complaint.

facts: A1 was alleged to have entered into an agreement with A2 to help him illegally acquire foreign exchange.
A2's scheme involved having a Swedish company (ASSAB) over-invoice goods, with the over-invoiced amount (40%) being credited to A2's account in a Swedish bank.
A1's role was to monitor this account in Sweden to confirm that the funds were being credited.
A1 allegedly traveled to India, brought A2 a statement of account, and stated he delivered it in person due to the sensitive nature of the transactions.
A1 also allegedly agreed to continue helping A2 with this scheme.
law: The relevant law is Section 120B of the Indian Penal Code, which pertains to the offense of criminal conspiracy.
The issue is whether the facts alleged in the complaint, if taken as true, are sufficient to charge a person under this section.
application: The Court determined that A1's alleged role was not passive but an "essential part of the agreement" and was "in furtherance of illegal and unlawful design to acquire foreign exchange."
A1's help was considered necessary for A2's plan, as A2 needed to know if the Swedish company was actually crediting his account.

The Court viewed A1's specific actions—such as keeping watch over the accounts, traveling to India, and personally delivering the bank statement—as overt acts performed as a consequence of the conspiracy agreement.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that, based on the allegations in the complaint, A1's actions constituted participation in a criminal conspiracy. Therefore, he could be charged with an offense under Section 120B of the Indian Penal Code.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a complaint under s. 23 (I )(b) cannot be launched before the Director of Enforcement has taken up the adjudication proceedings and made some inquiry in those proceedings and formed the opinion that it was necessary to have resort to the more drastic provision of conviction by a court.
appellant_arguments: The Director of Enforcement must first initiate adjudication proceedings.
Only after forming an opinion during those proceedings that the available penalty is inadequate can the Director file a criminal complaint.
Therefore, the current complaint is premature and must be quashed.
respondent_arguments: The indictment is for conspiracy (under the Indian Penal Code), which is a different offence from the substantive offences created by the special Act.
The procedural limitations of the special Act, such as the requirement for prior adjudication, do not apply to a separate charge of conspiracy.

arguments.issue_text: Whether A 1 can be charged in respect of acts alleged against him in the complaint.
appellant_arguments: Even if all the facts stated in the complaint are accepted as correct, they do not amount to an offence of conspiracy under s. 120B of the Indian Penal Code.
The alleged agreement and overt acts are, in reality, an offence under the special Act (s. 23 (IA)) and should be prosecuted under its specific procedures.
respondent_arguments: (Inferred) The facts alleged in the complaint are sufficient to make out a prima facie case for conspiracy under s. 120B of the Indian Penal Code, an offence distinct from any under the special Act.

cases.principle: When a statute makes unlawful that which was lawful before and appoints a specific remedy, that remedy and no other must be pursued.

cases.case_name: M/s. Rayala Corporation (P) Ltd. and anr. v. The Director of Enforcement; New Delhi
cases.principle: It was cited as laying down the rule to be followed for allowing the appeals.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: An agreement to commit illegal acts in the future does not, in itself, constitute an evasion or avoidance of the provisions of an Act, as the words "directly or indirectly" within the statute do not encompass such future agreements.
obiter: It is a fundamental principle of law that what cannot be done directly should not be permitted to be done indirectly.
The Director of Enforcement must first take up adjudication proceedings before making a complaint in writing to the Court.
An agreement with overt acts alleged for proving a conspiracy under s. 120-B I.P.C. is in reality an offence under s. 23 (IA) read with s. 21 (I).

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: A criminal complaint for conspiracy under the general penal code (s. 120B I.P.C.) is a distinct offense and is not barred by the procedural prerequisites, such as prior adjudication proceedings, that are required for prosecuting substantive offenses under the special Act. The procedural limitations of the special Act do not apply to a separate charge of conspiracy, even if the overt acts constituting the conspiracy are themselves violations of the special Act.
legal_tests_applied: The principle that a general offense (conspiracy under the Indian Penal Code) is distinct from a special offense (contravention of the Act) and is not governed by the procedural requirements of the special statute.
why_appellant_lost: The court rejected the argument that the complaint was premature. It held that the requirement to first initiate adjudication proceedings under the special Act applies only to substantive offenses under that Act, not to a separate and distinct charge of conspiracy under the Indian Penal Code.

The court rejected the contention that the alleged acts did not amount to a conspiracy. It found that the allegations—that appellant no. 2 asked appellant no. 1 to help him acquire foreign exchange illegally and appellant no. 1 agreed and continued to carry out the agreement—were sufficient to constitute a prima facie case for conspiracy.
The argument that the complaint was not bona fide and was filed for a collateral purpose was rejected.
why_respondent_won: The respondent successfully established that the indictment was for conspiracy under the Indian Penal Code, which is a different offense from the substantive contraventions created by the special Act.

Consequently, the court accepted that the procedural limitations of the special Act, specifically the requirement for prior adjudication before filing a complaint, do not apply to a separate charge of conspiracy.
The facts alleged in the complaint were deemed sufficient to make out a prima facie case for conspiracy, distinct from any offense under the special Act.
policy_considerations: Allowing the prosecution for conspiracy to proceed under the general penal code, even when the overt acts are violations of a special statute, prevents the procedural safeguards of the special statute from being used to shield individuals from prosecution for the separate and distinct offense of criminal agreement (conspiracy).
